cd /home/nab-raj.roshyara@dg-nexolution.de/roshyara/personal/nrna1/docs/knowledgeos/knowlegeos_manual_theory_20261018/06-theory/manuscript; python3 -I - <<'EOF'
p='chapter_01/CH-01-knowledge-authority-execution.md'; s=open(p).read()
R=[
("**Classification:** NEW IDEA; a gap in this book as well. Chapters 0–2 govern **standing** (what counts as authoritative) and **grant scope** (who may act). Neither says who may **know**.",
 "**Classification:** UPDATE OR REFINEMENT of §1.7. *(Revised R1-10: the first version said that \"Chapters 0–2 … neither says who may **know**\". That contradicted §1.7, which already gives the visibility rule vis(d) ⊆ ∩ vis(sᵢ) and treats visibility as a fourth label.)* What IA adds is that the **sources** of 08-16 had not yet turned §1.7's rule into a governed mechanism; the book's own model of read access is in §1.7."),
("- *Candidate* dimension: the confidentiality class of a claim. It is shown independent of **standing** only; it is **not tested** against the governed classification κ, which may already be able to carry it.",
 "- *Candidate* dimension: the confidentiality class of a claim. **This is the visibility label of §1.7** (\"visibility is a fourth label … orthogonal\"), stated from the grant side: vis(c) is the set of principals whose read grants cover *c*'s class. It is shown independent of **standing** only; it is **not tested** against the governed classification κ, which may already be able to carry it."),
("This rule is directly relevant to *this* research programme. The sealed and hold-out rules that currently block corpus reading are visibility rules in exactly this sense.",
 """**Necessary, not sufficient: inferred relationships (Src: AG L63–69; Ded; added R1-8).** A later source points out that "a graph projection must not reveal restricted relationships merely because the connected nodes themselves are visible", and that **an edge inferred from two visible nodes can disclose a restricted fact that neither node discloses alone** [AG L65, L69]. *Analysis (Ded):* the rule above bounds a derived item's visibility by its **sources**. It cannot see that a **combination** of permitted items may itself be sensitive: the aggregation problem known from database security. So the bound is **necessary but not sufficient**. Derived items (edges, chunks, summaries, assembled contexts) need their **own** visibility classification, which may be stricter than the intersection of their sources. Where no such classification exists, the safe reading is to treat the derived item as undetermined for visibility, not as visible.

This rule is directly relevant to *this* research programme. The sealed and hold-out rules that currently block corpus reading are visibility rules in exactly this sense."""),
("Each \"X ≠ authority\" is an instance of this theorem for one property X.",
 "Each \"X ≠ authority\" is an instance of this theorem for one property X. *(Example from a later source, added R1-9:* \"a similarity score is only a relevance signal. It is not permission, authority, applicability, or truth\" [AG L53]. In retrieval terms, embedding similarity measures topical closeness, not whether a claim **applies** here, **binds**, or is **true**. So ranking by similarity can only follow filtering by visibility, applicability and standing, never replace it.)"),
]
for a,b in R:
    assert s.count(a)==1,a[:50]; s=s.replace(a,b)
a="> - **DE**: `docs/knowledge_tranfer/20260816_1044_domain_events.md` (AI-generated, PROPOSED; with addenda on outbox and inbox; external citations unverified)"
s=s.replace(a,a+"\n> - **AG**: `docs/knowledge_tranfer/20260816_1057_artifact_gap_analysis.md` (AI-generated, PROPOSED; gap analysis of remaining artifacts)")
open(p,'w').write(s)
p='chapter_00/CH-00-foundations.md'; t=open(p).read()
a="**Open:** whether the corpus theory is about the theory layer, the platform, or the product. The corpus chapters must"
b="""**A compact statement of the target (Src, PROPOSED; AG L15–26; added R0-1).** A later source proposes defining the system not as "a set of services that store knowledge" but as **"a governed state-and-analysis system"**:

> authoritative knowledge + evidence + applicability + authority + temporal validity + formal analysis + governed resolution + traceable delivery.

*Analysis (Int).* Every term has a place in this book:
- authoritative knowledge → standing (Ch. 1 §1.2);
- evidence → evidential grade and epistemic support (§1.3);
- applicability → Ch. 2 §2.2, §2.8;
- authority → Ch. 1 §1.6, §1.14.1;
- temporal validity → Ch. 2 §2.11 and Ch. 1 §1.16.2;
- formal analysis → Ch. 2 §2.3–§2.7;
- governed resolution → dispositions by act (Ch. 2 §2.4);
- traceable delivery → context assembly and provenance (§0.7; Ch. 1 §1.16).

It is therefore a good one-line summary of the **platform** layer. It does not settle the open question below, which asks which layer the corpus theory is about.

**Open:** whether the corpus theory is about the theory layer, the platform, or the product. The corpus chapters must"""
assert t.count(a)==1; open(p,'w').write(t.replace(a,b)); print('ok')
EOF
